newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Union day of protest disrupts West Australia state.
newsitem.headline: Union day of protest disrupts West Australia state.

text.p: A 24-hour "day of action" on Tuesday to protest against proposed changes to Western Australia's state industrial relations laws produced widespread but patchy disruption of the state's economy, the Western Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (CCI) said.

A CCI spokesman said the effects varied depending mainly on the degree to which the workforce in different industries was unionised but the major concern for employers was the possibility of further action.
The state's trade union movement believes the new legislation is anti-union.
"The industrial action has created difficulties and some ongoing disruption but also what is happening is the unions have said that today is not going to be the end of it," he said.
"We're concerned there may be some further problems with transport for example in the next few days. Power is also a big concern."

The Labor Relations Legislation Amendment Bill was due to be introduced in the state's upper house, the Legislative Council, on Tuesday after passing through the lower house, the Legislative Assembly, earlier this month.

As well as providing for pre-strike secret ballots, the bill limits union access to work sites and non-union employee records and disallows political donations by unions without majority membership support.
The day of action included a rally of 20,000 unionists through Perth's central business district that police said disrupted traffic in the city.
In addition a 48-hour stoppage by Muja power station employees in Collie in the state's southwest was threatening to cause power restrictions from midnight tonight.

Industrial action in the transport sector prevented any commercial flights into or out of the state from midnight Monday night (1600 GMT) but a Qantas Airways Ltd spokesman said almost all its flights had been re-scheduled to minimise inconvenience and delays.
Ports were also targeted but the CCI spokesman said the impact had been minimal because of re-scheduling of vessels.
"The effect on construction was fairly considerable," he said. "Probably most of the big sites are operating at a low level or not at all.
"In the engineering and contracting sector the big fabricators have been affected to a varying degree depending on whether there is strong union representation in the workforce."
The spokesman said output in the manufacturing sector had been affected but not to a high degree, with most employers planning for some reduction in the workforce.
"A number of major mineral resources producers were not affected because they have (non-union) workplace agreements," the spokesman said.
